title: Snowmass Village Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Snowmass Village wells have a 145 ft median depth, with fractured bedrock, variable yields, and drilling costs of $15,400-$26,500 completed.
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Snowmass Village means understanding the well records before you rely on a listing's water claims. Within 5 miles of the village, Colorado Division of Water Resources records include 1,251 permitted wells. Of those, 601 are recorded as constructed, 702 report total depth, 224 report pump yield, and 51 report static water level.

The local ground is mountain bedrock, commonly granite or gneiss, and many permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. That geology can produce good wells, but results can change sharply between nearby lots. Use these records to set expectations, then verify the specific well, permit, pump equipment, and water quality before closing.

sections.heading: Snowmass Village well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Snowmass Village is 145 feet. The middle half runs from 75 to 300 feet, so a driller bidding a new well here should not assume every hole will resemble the median. The records include wells under 100 feet as well as wells deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,075 feet.

Depth is controlled by the local fractured-bedrock system rather than a uniform shallow aquifer. A well may encounter water along productive fractures, while another nearby hole may need to continue farther. For budgeting, ask for a written per-foot rate and a clear explanation of what happens if the hole must be deepened. Nearby records from Aspen, Woody Creek, Snowmass, and Basalt can provide context, but they do not guarantee a result on your parcel.

sections.heading: What Snowmass Village wells produce
sections.html:
Reported yields are generally strong, but the yield data covers only 224 wells. The median pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 8.9 to 15.0 gallons per minute. In the available records, 53% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 38% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 7% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That low-yield share is small, but it matters to a buyer because a single lot can still be an exception in fractured rock. Ask whether the reported figure is a test yield, a pump setting, or a long-term sustainable rate. Household-use wells are commonly exempt wells, but the permit controls allowed use, and the Colorado limit for exempt-well pumping is 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Snowmass Village water levels: useful records, limited trend
sections.html:
Among the 51 wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 40 feet. The middle half ranges from 18 to 94 feet. This gives a useful local starting point for estimating pumping and well-construction conditions, but it is not a promise about a particular lot. Static water level can vary with elevation, fracture location, season, and how long the well has rested.

The permit history is organized by issue decade, not by repeated water-level measurements. Because the available facts do not show static levels by decade, they do not establish that the water table is rising or dropping. For a purchase, obtain the well construction report and a current water-level check where possible. A driller or pump contractor can also evaluate whether the pump is set appropriately for the reported level.

sections.heading: Who drilled near Snowmass Village and when
sections.html:
Permit activity shows long-term development rather than a single recent building wave. Records include 3 permits from the 1950s, 45 from the 1960s, 171 from the 1970s, 155 from the 1980s, 292 from the 1990s, 213 from the 2000s, 100 from the 2010s, and 111 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most frequent driller names are Shelton Drilling Corporation, also listed as Shelton, Wayne, with 440 records; Collins Drilling Co, listed as Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” with 109; and Mountain Drilling Co., listed as Mcvey, Ora, with 86. These are permit-record counts, not endorsements or proof of current availability. Confirm the driller's present licensing, insurance, scope of work, and references before signing a contract.

sections.heading: What a new Snowmass Village well can cost
sections.html:
Fractured granite and gneiss make drilling slower and less predictable than work in uniform soft material. The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 145-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $9,400 to $14,500.

A finished system is estimated at about $15,400 to $26,500 after adding the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work. That range is a planning figure, not a fixed bid. Ask whether mobilization, casing, grout, difficult access, permits, water testing, storage, and rock excavation are included. On a steep lot near Snowmass Village, access and trenching can materially affect the final proposal even if the drilled depth matches the local median.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building or buying
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve attention because fractured-bedrock wells depend on intersecting productive fractures. The records show 2% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, but the yield sample is much smaller than the total permit count. A low-yield well may require storage and careful demand planning. Confirm the permit's allowed use, construction details, pump test, and any production problems.

Water quality also needs site-specific testing. Within about 10 miles, the mapping shows 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 112 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not prove contamination at your property, but they support testing before purchase. Check septic setbacks, drainfield space, slope stability, access for drilling equipment, and the feasibility of trenching utilities. Existing septic systems should be inspected rather than assumed sound.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Snowmass Village lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and construction records for the exact parcel. Compare the well's depth, static level, yield, pump, casing, grout, and permitted use with nearby records. The dominant permit use is domestic or household at 64%, while monitoring accounts for 19%, irrigation 4%, and stock 3%. Make sure the permit matches the home, occupancy, and planned landscaping.

For vacant land, have a driller review access, likely bedrock, siting, and a fallback plan before you close. For an existing home, test the water, document pressure and recovery, inspect the pump equipment, and verify septic capacity. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be needed for certain uses. Treat the well as part of the property's infrastructure, not as an automatic source of unlimited water.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Snowmass Village?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 145 feet, and the middle half of wells runs from 75 to 300 feet. The records also include wells deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest at 1,075 feet. Because Snowmass Village sits over fractured mountain bedrock, depth can vary substantially between nearby lots.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Snowmass Village?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 145-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,400 to $14,500. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $15,400 to $26,500. Difficult access or a deeper hole can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Snowmass Village?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 8.9 to 15.0 gallons per minute. More than 15 gallons per minute is reported by 53% of wells with yield records. However, only 224 wells report yield, and fractured-bedrock results can vary sharply from one property to another.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Snowmass Village?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or nearby yield record. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 112 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well before buying, including contaminants relevant to the property's location, and inspect the well and septic system.
